q: A Māori wayfinding practice turns silver-fern fronds pale-side upward for what purpose?
source: New Zealand Story · Silver fern history
evidenceRead: Government cultural account describes overturned fronds forming visible trail arrows by moonlight or torchlight.

q: Franklinia can put seed development on hold through winter. Which already-created cell waits without dividing?
source: Povilus and colleagues · Franklinia zygotic dormancy
evidenceRead: Primary paper abstract reports autumn fertilization followed by zygotic dormancy until spring.

q: The pink interior of an active bean-family root nodule comes from a protein related to which familiar blood protein?
source: New Mexico State University · Nitrogen fixation by legumes
evidenceRead: Extension publication states pink/red color comes from leghemoglobin, similar to blood hemoglobin, controlling oxygen flow to bacteria.

q: In an experiment with beach evening primroses, what changed after the flowers were exposed to nearby pollinator-like sounds?
source: Veits and colleagues · Flower response to pollinator sound
evidenceRead: Primary paper reports Oenothera drummondii petal vibration and rapid increased nectar sugar after bee and matched-frequency sounds.

q: The dangling, feathery structures beneath the floating fern Salvinia resemble roots. What are they actually?
source: University of Oxford · Salvinia molesta
evidenceRead: Oxford herbarium account describes two floating leaves and a third rootlike, divided, submerged leaf.

q: What unexpected genetic cargo has the flowering shrub Amborella accumulated inside its mitochondria?
source: Rice and colleagues · Amborella mitochondrial genomes
evidenceRead: Primary abstract reports foreign mitochondrial DNA from green algae, mosses and other angiosperms, including whole-genome transfers.

q: Cardamine chenopodiifolia hedges its reproductive bets by making fruits in which two places on the same plant?
source: Max Planck Institute · Amphicarpic development
evidenceRead: Institutional study account contrasts aerial explosive fruits and underground non-explosive fruits formed from buried self-pollinating flowers.

q: Where have researchers shown brewing yeast can spend the winter and then pass to a new insect generation?
source: Stefanini and colleagues · Wasps and yeast ecology
evidenceRead: Experiment demonstrated yeast persistence in adult overwintering Vespa and Polistes queens and transmission to progeny.

q: In germination experiments on Suaeda aralocaspica, how did its fresh brown and black seeds differ?
source: Wang and colleagues · Dimorphic desert seeds
evidenceRead: Primary experiment found brown seeds nondormant and black seeds with physiological dormancy; seed types differ in germination behavior.

q: What can a dried-out fairy-ring champignon mushroom do when rain returns?
source: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew · Fairy-ring champignon
evidenceRead: Kew account explicitly describes complete drying followed by expansion and regained shape after rain.

q: Some fungus-farming ants maintain helpful bacteria on their outer bodies. What service do those microbes provide?
source: Currie and colleagues · Ants’ bacterial housing
evidenceRead: Primary abstract describes antibiotic-producing bacteria in ant cuticular crypts supported by glands; related primary study PMID21106596 confirms defense against Escovopsis.

q: Leaf-cutting ants add fecal droplets to fresh leaves in their gardens. What useful material do these droplets recycle from the fungus they eat?
source: Rønhede and colleagues · Fungal enzymes in ant gardens
evidenceRead: Primary experiment identifies cell-wall-degrading enzymes of fungal rather than ant origin in fecal droplets.

q: The dyes in traditional litmus paper were extracted from what living material?
source: EMBL–EBI ChEBI · Litmus
evidenceRead: ChEBI chemical database defines litmus as a mixture of dyes extracted from several lichen species. Botanical garden account independently corroborates source.
qualification: Frozen raw source URL with encoded colon returned404. Parent repaired canonical source to Australian National Botanic Gardens lichen-dyeing page: https://cpbr.gov.au/lichen/lichens-people-dyeing.html. Do not import old raw URL over the parent repair.

q: What human-made debris has been found tangled in Mediterranean seagrass fiber bundles called Neptune balls?
source: Sanchez-Vidal and colleagues · Seagrasses trapping plastics
evidenceRead: Primary paper examines microplastics and larger plastic pieces in beached seagrass material; university release explicitly describes incorporation into fiber balls.

q: In a landmark Arizona murder investigation, DNA from which overlooked plant material helped connect a vehicle to the crime scene?
source: National Institute of Justice · Plant DNA evidence
evidenceRead: Official forensic training account identifies palo verde seedpod molecular identification linking suspect to particular crime scene.

q: How does the fungus Entomophthora muscae help infected female housefly corpses spread infection to healthy males?
source: Naundrup and colleagues · Fungus-driven fly attraction
evidenceRead: Primary study links fungal volatile blends and altered host hydrocarbons to male sexual attraction and infection.
qualification: Chemical attraction by dead infected female flies; distinct from card249 living infected males copying a female behavioral signal.

q: The ants living with Nepenthes bicalcarata can do what inside the plant’s fluid-filled pitchers?
source: Clarke and Kitching · Swimming ants and pitcher plants
evidenceRead: Primary study describes swimming ants hauling prey from pitcher fluid and consuming it.

q: Why can temporarily ineffective, dry pitcher-plant traps eventually catch more ants than continuously slippery traps?
source: Bauer and colleagues · Temporarily inactive pitcher traps
evidenceRead: Primary experiment and model support safe access for scouts promoting recruitment; framed as can, not deliberate planning.

q: Why can’t ordinary seed-bank drying and freezing preserve many oak acorns?
source: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew · Cryopreservation
evidenceRead: Kew states recalcitrant seeds die when fully dried and whole frozen acorns suffer lethal ice formation.

q: What unexpected growing position helped Kew propagate the tiny waterlily Nymphaea thermarum successfully?
source: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew · Nymphaea thermarum
evidenceRead: Historical cultivation account reports surface-level water and air exposure producing mature flowering plants; no current extinction-status claim.

q: The long twining part of a Lygodium climbing fern may look like a vine stem. What is it actually part of?
source: Mueller · Shoot morphology of Lygodium
evidenceRead: Primary morphology paper describes indeterminate leaves with shootlike continuous growth and circumnutation; Smithsonian flora corroborates twining frond axes.

q: What holds some lodgepole-pine cones shut for years until sufficient heat allows their seeds to escape?
source: National Park Service · Fire and lodgepole pine
evidenceRead: NPS describes cones sealed tightly with resin that melts during fire; scoped to some cones because serotiny varies.

q: Researchers proposed that pale patches on Caladium steudneriifolium leaves deter egg-laying moths by resembling what?
source: Soltau and colleagues · Defensive leaf variegation
evidenceRead: Primary study tests mine-like variegation and finds reduced herbivory; question preserves proposed interpretation.

q: What unusual process clears away the aging gills of the mushroom Coprinus comatus as its spores mature?
source: Australian National Botanic Gardens · Mushroom spore discharge
evidenceRead: Botanical garden account describes cap dissolving into an inky mess and dripping away; progressive tissue removal assists spore escape.

q: The white patches on a typical red fly-agaric mushroom cap are leftovers from what?
source: University of Wisconsin–Green Bay · Amanita descriptions
evidenceRead: University descriptions identify cap patches as universal-veil remnants; does not provide mushroom-eating guidance.

q: Some dramatically streaked tulips prized during Dutch tulip mania owed their patterns to what unexpected cause?
source: Royal Horticultural Society · Tulip viruses
evidenceRead: RHS ties tulip breaking virus and flower breaks to seventeenth-century tulipomania; not all striped modern tulips are infected.

q: During its heat-producing flowering phase, what does a sacred lotus do when the surrounding air becomes colder?
source: Seymour and Schultze-Motel · Lotus thermoregulation
evidenceRead: Primary abstract reports proportional increase in heat production as air cools and relatively stable flower temperatures; active regulation distinct from simple heating.

q: Bubbles can emerge from the center of a lotus leaf where water has collected. What internal process causes them?
source: Matthews and Seymour · Lotus gas canals
evidenceRead: Primary anatomy article describes gas bubbling through pools on lotus leaves and pressure-driven gas transport. Companion primary DOI10.1111/pce.12163 details leaf–petiole–rhizome ventilation.

q: Some fern colonies survive far beyond the range of the familiar leafy plants. Which living stage can make up these colonies?
source: American Fern Society · Independent fern generations
evidenceRead: Society account describes independent fern gametophyte populations beyond sporophyte ranges and species without known sporophytes.

q: In Charles and Francis Darwin’s grass-seedling experiments, shading which small region could prevent bending toward light?
source: Charles Darwin · The Power of Movement in Plants, pages 471–474
evidenceRead: Read primary1880 text pages471–474: opaque upper caps prevented or greatly reduced Phalaris bending; transparent caps did not; removing opaque caps restored response. Not a universal no-bending result.

q: The bizzaria citrus can produce citrons, sour oranges and strange mixed fruits on one plant. How was this combination created?
source: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew · Grafting
evidenceRead: Kew describes graft chimeras as two species combined without crossbreeding and specifically lists three fruit types on bizzaria.

q: In certain orchids, a pollen packet bends into its effective position only after riding on an insect for a while. What does that delay help prevent?
source: Plants · Orchid pollinarium reconfiguration study
evidenceRead: Field observations compared pollinator residence with pollinarium bending time; reconfiguration generally took longer, supporting avoidance of geitonogamy.

q: When scientists grew thale cress in actual Apollo Moon samples on Earth, what happened?
source: Communications Biology · Plants grown in Apollo lunar regolith
evidenceRead: Primary study reports growth in Apollo11/12/17 regolith, reduced development and stress-associated gene expression; experiment occurred on Earth.

q: Some bacteria living on leaves can make plants more vulnerable to a mild frost. What do these bacteria provide?
source: Plant Physiology · Bacterial ice nucleation and frost injury
evidenceRead: Primary1982 study states epiphytic ice-nucleating Pseudomonas syringae and Erwinia herbicola suffice to cause injury at minus5°C.

q: A grass living in hot soil gains heat tolerance from a fungus inside it. What must be living inside that fungus for the partnership to work?
source: USGS · Three-way symbiosis and thermal tolerance
evidenceRead: USGS primary paper abstract reports virus-cured fungal isolates cannot confer heat tolerance, and reintroduction restores it. PubMed direct view returned an empty disclosure page.

q: In experiments with soil microbes, what living structures helped swimming bacteria spread through spaces they otherwise struggled to cross?
source: Environmental Science & Technology · Taking the fungal highway
evidenceRead: Primary abstract in Swiss repository reports motile Achromobacter dispersal along Fusarium hyphae; liquid-film swimming is explicitly a proposed mechanism. PubMed page failed to display abstract.

q: The black nectar of Melianthus flowers uses chemistry resembling which traditional writing material?
source: New Phytologist · Black nectar chemistry in Melianthus
evidenceRead: Primary abstract identifies iron/ellagic-acid black pigment, peroxidase conversion and chemical analogy to iron-gall ink; no claim that bird attraction was directly demonstrated.

q: After snails ate two studied lichens, what unexpectedly regenerated from fragments in their droppings?
source: Annals of Botany · Lichen regeneration after snail ingestion
evidenceRead: Primary feeding experiment with Lobaria pulmonaria and Physcia adscendens found regenerating fragments in snail feces; preserves species scope.

q: A buffalo-bur flower has different kinds of pollen-bearing anthers. Experiments found a division of labor between pollinating other flowers and doing what?
source: Journal of Evolutionary Biology · Division of labor within flowers
evidenceRead: Primary Solanum rostratum/Bombus impatiens flight-cage experiments: feeding anthers manipulated preferentially; pollinating anthers export more pollen.

q: The pitcher plant Nepenthes aristolochioides has a translucent dome. How does that feature help catch insects?
source: Plant Signaling & Behavior · Light traps in Nepenthes
evidenceRead: Primary abstract: shading rear dome reduced Drosophila capture threefold relative to front-shaded/control pitchers. Full-paper indexed passage explicitly describes reversed orientation cue; PMC direct view CAPTCHA.

q: When a male wasp attempts to mate with a hammer orchid’s imitation female, what does the flower’s hinged lip do?
source: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew · Orchid pollination tricks
evidenceRead: Kew Drakaea account explicitly says labellum swings and flips male wasp onto stigma. Distinct from Catasetum launching a pollen packet at an insect.

q: A whitefly acquired a gene that helps it neutralize defensive chemicals in its food. From which kind of organism did that gene originate?
source: Cell · Plant-to-whitefly gene transfer
evidenceRead: Primary paper traces BtPMaT1 to plants and tests its defensive role using RNA interference; functional gene transfer rather than a general horizontal-transfer definition.

q: Apple leaf-miner larvae can maintain what unusual feature around their feeding sites as the rest of a leaf ages and yellows?
source: Proceedings of the Royal Society B · Leaf-miner green islands
evidenceRead: Primary Phyllonorycter blancardella experiment linked bacterial symbionts, probably Wolbachia, to green-island formation; wording does not assert all leaf miners or definitive bacterial identity.

q: After caterpillar attack, wild tobacco can change its flowers to favor hummingbirds over the moths that lay those caterpillars. What timing change was observed?
source: Current Biology · Herbivory changes tobacco pollination
evidenceRead: Primary abstract reports herbivory-induced morning opening and lower benzylacetone emission, with hummingbird rather than nocturnal hawkmoth visits.

q: When rootworms attack maize roots, a released chemical can recruit which underground allies?
source: Nature · Recruitment of nematodes by damaged maize roots
evidenceRead: Primary field and laboratory experiments identify root-emitted beta-caryophyllene attraction of entomopathogenic nematodes.

q: How can a tiny spherical cyanobacterium detect which direction light is coming from without having an eye?
source: eLife · Cyanobacteria use micro-optics to sense light direction
evidenceRead: Primary microscopy and phototaxis experiments show whole-cell lensing and focused spot opposite light source. Cyanobacterium explicitly labeled bacterium, not plant.

q: Diatom populations can gradually become smaller during repeated cell divisions. Which event can reset their size cycle?
source: Frontiers in Plant Science · Diatom sexual reproduction review
evidenceRead: Author review explains progressive population size reduction during vegetative divisions and size restoration by sexual auxospores; not every daughter cell shrinks every division.

q: Nathaniel Ward’s idea for enclosed plant cases grew from an accidental fern growing in a bottle. What had he originally placed in that bottle to observe?
source: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew · History of the Wardian case
evidenceRead: Kew historical account describes Ward’s1829 bottle with soil/fern fronds and moth cocoon; accidental fern growth led to enclosed plant transport.

q: Kew’s collection included a supposed bromeliad species that turned out to be a botanical hoax. How had its specimen been made?
source: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew · Botanical hoaxes
evidenceRead: Kew curatorial account identifies Quesnelia liboniana flowers inserted in a Vriesea rosette; only plant-hoax passage used.

q: Some tree species in Angola’s sandy highlands appear surprisingly small above the surface. Where is most of their woody structure?
source: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew · New species of2023
evidenceRead: Kew press account states multiple tree families in highland Angola evolved to be90percent or more underground; no unsupported single adaptive explanation asserted.

q: The giant sundew Drosera magnifica came to scientists’ attention through photographs posted on which online platform?
source: Phytotaxa · Description of Drosera magnifica
evidenceRead: Primary description PDF explicitly reports discovery via Facebook photographs. Avoids a broader claim of first-ever species discovered online.

q: A dried true rose of Jericho, Anastatica hierochuntica, can spread its branches when watered. What is actually moving?
source: Annals of Botany · Movement in Anastatica
evidenceRead: Primary anatomical paper states whole dead skeleton controls seed dispersal, with lignified conducting tissue bending dry and straightening wet. Distinct seed-preserving skeleton, not fossil cone opening.

q: Certain hungry fungi start building nematode traps after detecting which revealing sign of nearby prey?
source: Current Biology · Fungi eavesdrop on nematode pheromones
evidenceRead: Primary abstract reports ascaroside-induced trap morphogenesis across related fungi, restricted to nutrient deprivation. Distinct from inflation mechanism in frozen botany17.

q: Some fungi form tiny balls that termites carefully tend in their nurseries. What do the balls impersonate?
source: Current Biology · Cuckoo fungus and termite eggs
evidenceRead: Primary abstract reports Reticulitermes sclerotia kept alongside eggs and tended only when fungus produces beta-glucosidase; chemical egg recognition directly tested.

q: Some Serapias orchids gain pollination visits by supplying male bees with what unusual resource?
source: Acta Botanica Neerlandica · Sleeping bees in Serapias flowers
evidenceRead: Primary1981 observations at two Israeli sites found male bees sleeping in Serapias vomeracea; flowers warmed above ambient in morning sun.

q: Fossil Xinicaulis trees widened their trunks in a startling way. What happened to the network of woody strands inside them as they grew?
source: Chinese Academy of Sciences · Fossil tree growth
evidenceRead: Research institution’s account of2017 PNAS study explicitly describes hollow cylindrical woody skeleton tearing and collapsing as diameter expanded.

q: Roots release strigolactone signals that help establish partnerships with fungi. Which unwelcome neighbors can exploit those same signals to start growing?
source: Annals of Botany · Strigolactone signaling review
evidenceRead: Author review covers strigolactones as AM-fungus recognition signals and Striga/Orobanche germination stimulants. PMC direct view CAPTCHA; indexed text and PubMed abstract read.

q: Research on wild yeasts found some heritable traits carried by changes in what, without a corresponding change in DNA sequence?
source: Nature · Prion inheritance in wild yeasts
evidenceRead: Primary survey of wild Saccharomyces finds self-templating prion conformations and conditionally beneficial heritable phenotypes; no claim all prions are beneficial.

q: Chemical analysis of cicadas infected with Massospora fungi uncovered which surprising class of compounds?
source: Fungal Ecology · Alkaloids in cicada pathogens
evidenceRead: Primary metabolomics identifies cathinone and psilocybin in different cicada–Massospora pairs; avoids asserting drug-driven behavioral mechanism.
qualification: Fungal alkaloids measured; mechanism of behavioral manipulation not asserted. Distinct from card249 signal observation.

q: The South African rat’s-tail plant grows a tall, bare stalk that carries no flowers. What useful service does this stalk provide?
source: Nature · Specialized bird perch in Babiana
evidenceRead: Primary Babiana ringens study identifies sterile inflorescence axis functioning exclusively as bird perch and positioning malachite sunbirds for cross-pollination.

q: The orchid Acampe rigida flowers when insect visits are scarce. What can physically move its pollen into its own stigma?
source: Annals of Botany · Rain pollination in Acampe
evidenceRead: Primary observations and rain-shelter experiments describe drop-driven cap removal, pollen ejection and elastic return to stigma; no autonomous self-pollination without rain.

q: Without a visiting insect, the orchid Holcoglossum amesianum can pollinate itself through which unusual movement?
source: Nature · Self-pollination in Holcoglossum
evidenceRead: Primary abstract describes anther turning360degrees against gravity into own stigmatic cavity, with no agent or medium.

q: A 2016 study found an additional fungal resident embedded in the outer layer of many lichens. What was this overlooked resident?
source: Science · Additional yeast partners in lichens
evidenceRead: Primary paper abstract at University of Glasgow repository reports specific basidiomycete yeasts in cortex across many lichens; no assertion all lichens require this third partner.

q: A crypt-keeper wasp develops inside another wasp living in an oak gall. What temporary exit plug does the parasite eventually chew through?
source: Proceedings of the Royal Society B · Crypt-keeper wasp manipulation
evidenceRead: Primary Bassettia pallida/Euderus set study documents manipulated emergence drilling, head plugging and parasite escape; plant-gall ecological interaction.

q: Some acacias make their protective ants more dependent on them by interfering with which ability of the ants?
source: Ecology Letters · Nectar-mediated partner dependence
evidenceRead: Primary paper reports nectar chitinase inhibits Pseudomyrmex gut invertase after workers’ first nectar meal; dependence on sucrose-free host nectar.

q: Some Macaranga trees protect their resident ants with a barrier that excludes many other climbing insects. What forms this barrier?
source: Oecologia · Macaranga wax barriers
evidenceRead: Primary study and Cambridge biomechanics research account describe epicuticular wax blooms excluding generalists while symbiotic ants climb effectively.

q: Ants living inside the hollow leaves of Dischidia major supply more than discarded food. Which gas from the colony can the plant recycle?
source: Nature · Ant-derived carbon in Dischidia
evidenceRead: Primary stable-isotope study estimates39percent leaf carbon from ant-related respiration; no precision required in card.

q: Inside some swollen ant-plants, smooth chambers serve as nurseries while warty chambers receive rubbish. What useful job do the warty surfaces perform?
source: National University of Singapore · Rubiaceous ant-plants
evidenceRead: Museum botanical account contrasts smooth chambers with highly absorptive lenticel-like warts at waste deposits; lowland Hydnophytum not generalized to all chambers.

q: What cue can Cayratia tendrils use when deciding whether to curl around another plant’s leaf?
source: Proceedings of the Royal Society B · Tendril contact chemistry
evidenceRead: Primary experiments show avoidance of oxalate-coated sticks and correlation with leaf oxalate content; contact chemoreception supported, not consciousness.

q: Which parts of a bumblebee can act as tiny moving sensors of a flower’s weak electric field?
source: PNAS · Bumblebee mechanosensory hairs
evidenceRead: Primary study measures electromechanical hair deflection and corresponding neural activity; related commentary distinguished hairs from antennae.

q: A 2023 study challenged the usual explanation for the crystal-like bladder cells on quinoa and common ice plant. What major function did the experiments reveal?
source: Current Biology · Epidermal bladder cell defenses
evidenceRead: Primary2023 study reports minor/absent abiotic protection and chemical/physical herbivore barrier; explicitly framed as study-specific revision, not broad universal rejection.

q: Which feature of sea rocket fruit helps some seeds travel while others stay close to the parent?
source: Brazilian Journal of Botany · Cakile fruit dispersal
evidenceRead: Primary Cakile maritima study: distinct upper/lower segments, upper dispersal versus seedlings near parent chiefly from lower segments; Bath thesis corroborates retention. Existing11813 only identifies species.

q: In a laboratory evolution study, some populations of single-celled green algae gained protection from predators by evolving what arrangement?
source: Scientific Reports · Predation and multicellularity
evidenceRead: Primary2019 experiment: two of five selected populations evolved multicellularity; assays supported protection. Not all populations and not instantaneous transformation.

q: In experiments on yellow Lantana flowers, what tiny event was enough to trigger a color change?
source: Journal of Experimental Botany · Lantana flower color
evidenceRead: Primary1984 experiment reports even one pollen grain sufficient and pollen extract mimicking effect. No unsupported claim all color change requires pollination.

q: Male and female shoots of one studied moss attract tiny animal visitors with different versions of what signal?
source: Nature · Sex-specific moss scents
evidenceRead: Primary Ceratodon purpureus study measures sex-specific volatile cues, differential microarthropod attraction and improved fertilization; terrestrial scent system distinct from algal waterborne sperm transport.

q: Roridula traps insects on sticky leaves but lacks the usual means to digest them itself. Which partners help it obtain nutrients from the catch?
source: Oecologia · Roridula digestive mutualism
evidenceRead: Primary Roridula dentata/Pameridea paper identifies obligate digestive mutualism and lack of digestive enzymes; foliar absorption supported independently by PMID15728666.

q: Male Welwitschia cones contain a sterile ovule-like structure. Instead of producing a seed, what does it offer insect visitors?
source: Kirstenbosch · Cultivation of Welwitschia
evidenceRead: Kirstenbosch author describes sterile modified pistil-like structure exuding nectar. SANBI indexed page corroborates; SANBI direct HTTP403 and later PDF find timed out after successful open.

q: The orchid Epipactis veratrifolia tricks female hoverflies into laying eggs on its flowers. What larval food does it falsely advertise?
source: BMC Evolutionary Biology · Aphid mimicry in an orchid
evidenceRead: Primary2014 report says aphid coloring and alarm pheromone mimicry induces hoverfly oviposition on false brood sites. Target false nursery distinct from attacked-bee smell luring adult food thieves.

q: In very dense experimental rows, neighboring sunflowers improved their access to light by arranging their stems into what pattern?
source: PNAS · Self-organization of sunflower stands
evidenceRead: Primary field study shows alternating stem inclinations propagating along high-density rows via red/far-red responses; distinct from daily tracking and mature heads facing east.

q: Laser scans of silver birches in calm weather revealed what subtle overnight change in their branches?
source: TU Wien · Overnight movement of birch trees
evidenceRead: First-party research account describes two birches, calm conditions without condensation, gradual night drooping and morning return; internal clock versus sunlight unresolved.

q: What can make a marimo algae ball rise through the water when it receives light?
source: University of Bristol · Floating marimo
evidenceRead: First-party2018 research account describes oxygen bubbles, inhibitor experiment and circadian effects; card targets bubble mechanism only.

q: Scientists tagged moss balls on an Alaskan glacier and watched them travel. What surprising pattern did the balls’ movements show?
source: Polar Biology · Movement of glacier moss balls
evidenceRead: Primary2020 study reports herd-like motion on Root Glacier, first south then southwest, associated with ablation. No claimed conscious coordination or complete explanation.

q: The tropical vine Marcgravia evenia grows a dish-shaped leaf above its flowers. What does this leaf reflect especially effectively?
source: Science · Echo-reflecting leaf in Marcgravia
evidenceRead: Primary acoustic measurements and behavioral experiments establish distinctive multidirectional echo and reduced bat foraging time.

q: In studied staghorn fern colonies, upper plants help catch leaf litter. What do the thicker fronds of lower plants particularly help store?
source: Behavioral Ecology · Division of labor in staghorn ferns
evidenceRead: Primary2024/2025 field and glasshouse study: thicker lower fronds with larger spaces facilitate captured rainwater storage; avoids asserting fully equivalent insect eusociality.

q: The orchid Dracula lafleurii attracts certain flies by imitating what in both appearance and smell?
source: New Phytologist · Mushroom mimicry in Dracula orchids
evidenceRead: Primary study used3D-printed molds and scent-free silicone flowers; supports size,shape,color,scent mimicry of mushrooms and mushroom-associated fly pollinators.

q: Many waterfall plants in the family Podostemaceae spend their growing season underwater. When do they typically expose their flowers?
source: National Museum of Nature and Science, Japan · River-weeds
evidenceRead: Museum botanical database describes submerged rainy-season growth and dry-season emergence; Kew flora corroborates aerial flowering and fruiting at low water.

q: Which organism survived simulated Martian conditions in a 2024 study and could regenerate after being returned to favorable conditions?
source: The Innovation · Extreme tolerance of desert moss
evidenceRead: Primary paper reports desiccated Syntrichia survival and regeneration following Mars-like chamber exposure; no actual Mars mission or demonstrated long-term Martian growth.

q: A 2011 study found which photosynthetic partners living inside cells of developing spotted salamander embryos?
source: PNAS — Kerney et al., 2011
evidenceRead: Primary abstract read in indexed PubMed result: imaging and algal DNA amplification demonstrate invasion of embryonic salamander tissues and cells. Direct page returned minimal footer; PMC open challenged.
qualification: Parent canonical wording says photosynthetic organisms, avoiding an unproven claim of mutual benefit. Raw retains earlier wording; preserve parent canonical version.

q: A 2018 plant study found that which familiar animal nerve-signaling chemical can also trigger a long-distance wound response in plants?
source: Science · Glutamate as a plant wound signal
evidenceRead: Primary study shows glutamate-triggered receptor-like channels and long-distance intracellular calcium propagation; no plant neurons or consciousness asserted.

q: Researchers could temporarily stop a Venus flytrap’s touch-triggered closure by exposing it to what kind of chemical?
source: Annals of Botany · Anesthetics and plant movement
evidenceRead: Primary study reports reversible movement inhibition and loss of flytrap action potentials under ether; no instructions or inference of animal-like awareness.

q: In a thale-cress experiment, what traveled down the stem and directly activated light receptors in underground roots?
source: Science Signaling · Stem-piped light
evidenceRead: Primary Arabidopsis experiment demonstrates stem-conducted light activating root phytochromeB and downstream root-growth responses.

q: Scientists recreated a cyanobacterial daily clock outside living cells using a mixture of what, supplied with ATP energy?
source: Science · Reconstituted cyanobacterial clock
evidenceRead: Primary2005 paper reconstitutes KaiC phosphorylation rhythm with KaiA,KaiB,KaiC and ATP; temperature compensation observed.

q: In warnowiid dinoflagellates, where is the elaborate lens-and-retina-like ocelloid assembled?
source: Nature · Components of dinoflagellate ocelloids
evidenceRead: Primary microscopy and genomics identify subcellular eye analogues including mitochondrial cornea-like layer and plastid retinal body. Does not assert human-like image perception.

q: One mathematical explanation for holes in Monstera leaves concerns making better use of which unreliable forest resource?
source: The American Naturalist · Monstera leaf fenestration model
evidenceRead: Primary2013 model links fenestration to reduced variance in growth under unpredictable sunflecks; model explicitly qualified.

q: Dodder can send tiny RNA molecules into a host plant. What did researchers find these particular molecules could do there?
source: Nature · Dodder microRNAs targeting host genes
evidenceRead: Primary Cuscuta campestris study shows trans-species regulation of host gene expression; functional targeting differs from general bidirectional messenger-RNA exchange in botany27.

q: Why can ethanol-rich wood be useful to certain fungus-farming ambrosia beetles?
source: PNAS · Alcohol and ambrosia beetle farming
evidenceRead: Primary experiments find ethanol boosts selected Ambrosiella/Raffaelea and inhibits competing Aspergillus/Penicillium; no claim all ethanol concentrations help.

q: Blue cohosh appears to bear small blue berries. What are those structures actually?
source: Missouri Botanical Garden · Blue cohosh
evidenceRead: Botanical garden explicitly describes berry-like seeds with fleshy blue outer coating;1927 Canadian government botany source corroborates early rupture of ovary.

q: Researchers tracking fruit-eating animals in flooded Amazonian forests documented long-distance seed dispersal by which group?
source: Proceedings of the Royal Society B · Amazonian fish seed dispersal
evidenceRead: Primary Colossoma tracking and gut-retention study supports viable seed transport; distances modeled, not every seed directly tracked.

q: Photosynthetic tissues under some tree bark recycle carbon dioxide from which nearby source?
source: Plant Physiology · Photosynthesis beneath eucalyptus bark
evidenceRead: Primary stable-isotope study of Eucalyptus miniata and introduction identify corticular refixation of internally respiredCO2; no gross claim allbark green.

q: An anther-smut infection can make female white campion flowers develop male-like anthers. What fills those altered structures?
source: Planta · Fungus-induced anthers in female campion
evidenceRead: Primary developmental study reports female Silene latifolia anther-like structures filled with Microbotryum spores rather than pollen.

q: What clue in Permian fossil leaves suggested that the leaves had been folded when insects fed on them?
source: Current Biology · Fossil evidence of leaf folding
evidenceRead: Primary2023 study interprets symmetrical insect feeding damage in mature gigantopterid leaves as evidence of folding; inference stated, not direct observation of ancient night behavior.

q: Some tropical orchids live without functional leaves. Which exposed organs can perform their photosynthesis instead?
source: Plant Physiology · Photosynthesis in leafless orchid roots
evidenceRead: Primary Campylocentrum tyrridion study measures rootCAM carbon exchange despite absence of stomata; clear leafless species scope.

q: One citrus seed can produce several seedlings, some of which match the mother plant genetically. Where do those clone embryos originate?
source: University of Florida IFAS · Citrus propagation
evidenceRead: UF extension explains polyembryony and maternal nucellar embryos; UCR primary proceedings distinguish gametic and nucellar embryos in same seed.

q: Cholla cacti can hitchhike on passing animals and establish new plants elsewhere. What are these spiny travelers?
source: National Park Service · Cholla cactus
evidenceRead: NPS describes detachedstem attachment to people/animals and primary reproduction when segmentsroot. Replaces albino-redwood proposedfact as too similar to kauri-root subsidy.

q: What change does an individual avocado flower normally make between its first and second openings?
source: University of California, Riverside — Avocado Flowering Basics
evidenceRead: University avocado collection page read, lines67–72: the same flower first opens female, closes, and reopens in its male phase. A/B types differ in timing.
qualification: Parent canonical answer shortened to Female function to male function. Preserve parent canonical version.

q: How can a field poppy prevent its own incompatible pollen from completing fertilization?
source: Plant Physiology · Wilkins et al., 2015
evidenceRead: Primary abstract read: Papaver rhoeas self-incompatibility triggers pollen programmed cell death; cytosolic acidification is essential to the process.
qualification: Restricted to self-incompatibility response in field poppy; not a universal plant response.

q: In experiments with Tasmanian Richea scoparia, snow skinks helped the plant reproduce by doing what to its flowers?
source: Biological Journal of the Linnean Society · Olsson et al., 2000
evidenceRead: Publisher-indexed abstract and quoted paper abstract read: nectar-foraging skinks tear off calyptra; removal facilitates seed release. Direct publisher open returns403; not presented as proven pollen-carrying.
qualification: Primary publisher-indexed abstract supports cap removal and seed release; direct publisher access403. Does not assert proven pollen carriage.

q: In studied wild Bolivian chilies, capsaicin helped protect the seeds against what attacker?
source: University of Washington · Bugs put the heat in chili peppers
evidenceRead: First-party research account read: capsaicinoids inhibit Fusarium entering insect-damaged fruit; birds disperse seeds without capsaicin pain.
qualification: Wild Bolivian chili study; not a universal explanation of all pungent fruits.

q: In tracer experiments, root-associated Metarhizium fungi supplied plants with nitrogen from which unusual source?
source: Applied and Environmental Microbiology · Behie and Bidochka, 2014
evidenceRead: Primary indexed research read: nitrogen-15 injected wax-moth larvae supplied nitrogen transferred by five Metarhizium species. Direct PubMed open challenged.
qualification: Nitrogen tracer evidence; revised stem removes answer giveaway. Root association and insect infection are both involved.

q: Experiments on Epichloë grass fungi found that which material from visiting flies could cross-fertilize another fungal individual?
source: Mycological Research · A new kind of mutualism between fungi and insects
evidenceRead: Primary indexed abstract read: flies cross-fertilize Epichloë; experimentally transferring fly feces to unfertilized stromata caused fertilization. Direct PDF request returned publisher navigation.
qualification: Experimentally transferred feces produced fertilization. Do not generalize this into an obligatory fly dependence for all Epichloë fungi. Primary indexed abstract read; direct PDF resolves to publisher navigation.

q: Pain-inducing miniproteins in Australian stinging trees have a folded structure resembling what?
source: Science Advances · Gilding et al., 2020
evidenceRead: Primary abstract/full indexed paper read: Dendrocnide gympietides have inhibitory cystine-knot folds shared with spider/cone-snail toxins and affect sodium channels.
qualification: Structural similarity of venom-like peptides, not evidence of animal origin.

q: How can the walls of many pollen grains protect their contents as the grains dry out during travel?
source: PNAS · Katifori et al., 2010
evidenceRead: Primary abstract read: compliant elongated apertures permit predictable reversible pollen-wall folding; sculpturing assists closure and prevents mirror buckling.
qualification: Wall geometry and reversible folding differ from sibling engineered pollen-paper humidity response.

q: The blue color of many bigleaf hydrangeas depends on taking up which metal from the soil?
source: Biometals · Schreiber et al., 2011
evidenceRead: Primary abstract read: red, purple and blue Hydrangea macrophylla sepals differed in aluminum content; aluminum–anthocyanin mixtures reproduced their spectra. University extension sources explain soil-pH effects on aluminum availability.
qualification: Verified journal corrected to Biometals. Primary abstract directly supports aluminum/color relationship; university accounts support soil availability context.

q: What surprising change can rain cause in the normally white petals of Diphylleia grayi?
source: Journal of Materials Chemistry A · Yong et al., 2015
evidenceRead: Research-paper introduction read in indexed PDF: white-to-transparent rain response arises when water fills intercellular spaces and reduces refractive-index contrast. Botanical observation is background, not the paper’s original experiment.
qualification: Natural botanical observation appears in introduction of an engineering paper; not presented as that paper’s original botanical experiment. Indexed PDF read.

q: Kelp stores iodide that researchers found can perform what protective chemical job?
source: PNAS · Küpper et al., 2008
evidenceRead: Primary abstract read: X-ray spectroscopy identifies accumulated iodide; it scavenges reactive oxygen species and effluxes under oxidative stress; antioxidant biological role proposed.
qualification: Antioxidant role supported by study; do not frame iodide as the only antioxidant in kelp.

q: Microscope experiments found that airborne mushroom spores can encourage which weather-related process?
source: PLOS ONE · Hassett et al., 2015
evidenceRead: Primary abstract read: environmental electron microscopy demonstrated droplet reformation on spores; rainfall promotion is proposed, not directly measured. Distinct from Buller-drop launch55.
qualification: Droplet condensation observed microscopically; rainfall promotion is a proposed consequence. Different from spores launching via droplet merger (card55) and mushroom convection (card4).

q: Cells shed from pea and corn root tips build external protective traps containing which surprising molecule?
source: Applications in Plant Sciences · Wen et al., 2017
evidenceRead: Primary abstract read: DNA-specific staining visualized extracellular structures; DNase altered them; no extracellular DNA accompanied killed cells.
qualification: Observed extracellular DNA in root-border-cell traps from studied species; not a generic assertion about all roots.

q: Besides attracting pollinators, larger ultraviolet pigment patterns in studied sunflower petals were linked with which benefit?
source: eLife · Genetic basis and dual adaptive role of floral pigmentation in sunflowers
evidenceRead: Primary paper read: largerUV patterns correlated with arid sites and desiccation resistance; reduced field transpiration is inferred from proxy measurements, retained as linked/proposed.
qualification: Pattern/water-loss association and proposed function retained; does not assert an experimentally established evolutionary explanation.

q: As many seeds dry out, their cell contents can assume what unusual physical state?
source: Comptes Rendus Biologies · Buitink and Leprince, 2008
evidenceRead: Authoritative review abstract read: orthodox-seed cytoplasm becomes glassy during drying; primary corn-embryo paper PMID16666651 independently measures glass transitions. Not all seeds tolerate drying.
qualification: Drying is used instead of dormancy. Authoritative review and independent primary corn-embryo evidence support glassy state; not all seeds tolerate drying.

q: Macropis bees collect oil from loosestrife flowers. Besides feeding their young, what do they use this oil to do?
source: Ecology and Evolution · Radchenko et al., 2025
evidenceRead: Primary paper indexed full-text read: pure floral oil brought to nests waterproofs new cell walls; study examines Lysimachia–Macropis collecting structures.
qualification: Floral oil lining nest chambers is distinct from ordinary nectar reward and from nonfloral plant resins.

q: In tapegrass, Vallisneria, what leaves the male plant and travels to female flowers at the water surface?
source: University of New Hampshire · Phycokey Vallisneria
evidenceRead: University morphology account fully read: detached male flowers rise, expose anthers/pollen and contact female flowers along the water-surface slope.
qualification: Detached whole male flowers in Vallisneria; distinct from seagrass submerged pollination.

q: In a 2021 experiment, electrical activity in Venus flytraps produced what detectable effect outside their tissues?
source: Scientific Reports · Fabricant et al., 2021
evidenceRead: Primary abstract read: optically pumped atomic magnetometers recorded biomagnetism accompanying heat-induced action potentials. No claim of plant magnetoreception.
qualification: Measures biomagnetic field associated with electrical impulses; no plant magnetic sensing claim.

q: A 2024 forest study found that microbes associated with tree bark can remove which greenhouse gas directly from the air?
source: University of Birmingham · Tree bark removes atmospheric methane
evidenceRead: First-party account and primary Nature paper DOI10.1038/s41586-024-07592-w read: upland woody surfaces consume methane, isotope/core tests support methanotrophy. Does not claim all trees are always sinks.
qualification: Study-specific woody methane uptake attributed to associated microbes; no blanket claim that every tree is a net methane sink.

q: Lab-grown Ulva seaweed can develop an abnormal body when deprived of which tiny partners?
source: Annals of Botany · Bacteria-induced morphogenesis of Ulva
evidenceRead: Primary indexed paper read: bacteria individually and paired induce distinct growth/morphogenesis functions in U.mutabilis and U.intestinalis; normal culture morphology requires suitable signals.
qualification: Study of bacteria-dependent Ulva morphology; no assertion that exactly two bacterial species are universally obligatory.

q: What powers green algal growth deep inside some caves opened to tourists?
source: National Park Service · Making the Cave Less Green
evidenceRead: First-party park ecologist account read: algae,moss,bacteria grow beside artificial lamps; unnatural food sources and speleothem damage motivate management.
qualification: Artificial lighting is the energy input; tourist caves specifically, not all green growth at cave entrances.

q: The silvery crust exuded by some alpine saxifrages contains vaterite, an unusual form of which substance?
source: Cambridge University Botanic Garden · Saxifraga sempervivum
evidenceRead: First-party botanical-garden research account read: S.sempervivum protectivecrust contains calcium-carbonatepolymorphvaterite exudedbyhydathodes.
qualification: Vaterite-containing crust in identified saxifrages; not merely the usual shell-calcium-carbonate identification.

q: Some naturally blue-green pieces of decaying wood are prized by craftspeople. What creates their color?
source: University of Gothenburg · Green elfcup fungus
evidenceRead: University fungal researcher’s field account fully read: Chlorociboria aeruginascens pigments rottingwood; stainedwood morecommonthanfruitbodies andvaluedincarpentry.
qualification: Pigment from wood-colonizing fungi, distinct from external fungal digestion (published670) and coral-fungus naming question2480.

q: When a bird bites an edible stamen appendage of an Axinaea flower, how does the flower shoot pollen onto the bird?
source: Current Biology · Dellinger et al., 2014
evidenceRead: Primary publisher abstract read: bird compression of aerenchymatous appendage forcesair into hollowanther, ejectingpollen; distinctfrompublished2482speciesidentity.
qualification: Air-bellows pollen jet from a bitten edible appendage; distinct from bird weight exposing anthers (nature0184) and Hypenia blasts removing rival pollen (card63).

q: Male periodical cicadas with an infectious stage of Massospora fungus were observed making which misleading signals?
source: Scientific Reports · Cooley et al., 2018
evidenceRead: Primary abstract read: males carrying conidiospores made precisely timed female-specific wing flicks; males with resting-spore infections did not. This behavioral observation differs from the alkaloid finding in card179.
qualification: Conidiospore-stage male wing flicks; stage specificity preserved. Closest similarity is card136, but living-male behavioral mimicry is distinct from corpse chemical attraction. Alkaloid179 teaches a separate observation.

q: In a letter about testing whether sensitive plants responded to sound, Charles Darwin mentioned trying sustained notes from which instrument?
source: Darwin Correspondence Project · Letter to John Tyndall, 4 December 1878
evidenceRead: The indexed primary letter and Cambridge editorial notes describe prolonged bassoon notes and a request for a siren. No claim of demonstrated plant hearing; the correspondence introduction records a later withdrawal.
qualification: Primary letter documents an attempted bassoon experiment, not demonstrated plant hearing. Later withdrawal noted in scholarly correspondence introduction.
